title: The evening examen
hook: where was God today? where did I love? where did I fail?
tomorrow: what deadline does the Bible put on anger?

segments.voice: Yesterday, one kindness, aimed at one person, a coat at a time: one a day. Tonight, a look back over the whole day.

Lying in bed, the day on a loop: what you said, what you should have said, what they meant by that. Paul seems to point two ways about it. To the church at Corinth he writes, “Examine yourselves, whether ye be in the faith; prove your own selves.” And in his earlier letter to the same church: “yea, I judge not mine own self,” because “he that judgeth me is the Lord.” So which is it? Look hard at your day, or hand the judging over?
screen: `THE DAY ON A LOOP.` → `EXAMINE YOURSELVES?` → `OR I JUDGE NOT MINE OWN SELF?`

segments.voice: Christians keep both lines, and they lean differently. One side builds a nightly habit on the first. Ignatius of Loyola wrote a short review of the day into his Spiritual Exercises: the examen. Its best case: a day nobody looks at tends to repeat itself, and God may have been in it unnoticed. Three questions carry it. Where was God today? Where did I love? Where did I fail? Luke's Emmaus story shows why looking back works. Two disciples realize only afterward, “Did not our heart burn within us, while he talked with us by the way?” They saw it on the replay. The other side is wary. For some Christians, a nightly self-review can slide into anxious scorekeeping, a courtroom in the head every night. Their best case is Paul's own: I judge not mine own self; the Lord does. Hand it over and rest. Here's where they meet. Ignatius's examen doesn't start with failures. It starts with thanks for this particular day's gifts, and it ends by asking pardon and looking to tomorrow. A review, not a trial. Both sides agree the day belongs to God. They differ on how closely to read it.
screen: `THE EXAMEN: WHERE WAS GOD?` · `SEEN ON THE REPLAY, LIKE EMMAUS.` · `THE WORRY: A COURTROOM AT NIGHT.` · `THANKS FIRST: A REVIEW, NOT A TRIAL.` · then, large: `WHERE WAS HE?`

segments.voice: Count on your fingers three good things from today, small ones included: a joke, a meal, a message. Then walk the hours back from now to waking and ask the three questions once each, without holding court. If you pray, end by handing the day over; if not, end where you began, on the thanks.
The evening examen. A short review of the day at night: thanks first, then where was God, where did I love, where did I fail.
Your line: where was he? Asked after the thanks, it's a replay, not a trial. Good night for now.

screen: `DAY 1690 COUNTS.` → `LIVING IT · 9 OF 70.` → `TOMORROW: WHAT DEADLINE DOES THE BIBLE PUT ON ANGER?`

howItsDone: Christians who pray the examen take a few minutes, often at night: thanks for the day, a walk back through its hours, a request for pardon, and a look toward tomorrow; others end the day simply by handing it to God.

notes: Written 2026-10-13 in the year-2-4 recipe; rewritten 2026-10-15 in recipe v3 (shape: debate; Grace: Grace was sharp back at Pop; in bed she replays the day for hours).

Debate shape: two real views inside the tradition, from two of Paul's lines (2 Corinthians 13:5 and 1 Corinthians 4:3–4): a nightly examen versus wariness of anxious self-scrutiny. Both are given their best case; neither is ranked. 'For some Christians, a nightly self-review can slide into anxious scorekeeping' describes a pastoral concern (scrupulosity), not a church's teaching; confirm it reads fairly.
The three questions come from the outline, not verbatim from Ignatius. Spiritual Exercises 43 is paraphrased: thanks first, then light, review, pardon, and resolve for tomorrow.
Year one taught the examen (day 102: Ignatius's conversion, Psalm 139:23, the five steps); this day avoids that story and verse.
'His earlier letter to the same church' = 1 Corinthians before 2 Corinthians, by their usual order; confirm the wording.
